initial_requirements: Small and medium businesses need Mashbot to manage their presence across multiple social networks through a consistent service. Staff should be able to connect external accounts, prepare campaigns, schedule content for simultaneous publication, manage contributor, approver, and publisher roles, respond to audience activity, and monitor keywords and campaign history. The service should reduce the effort required to coordinate marketing and customer engagement across changing platforms.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What are the primary business goals Mashbot must achieve for small and medium businesses, and which core user capabilities are most important to support those goals?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
The main business goal is to help small and medium businesses manage social media more efficiently without needing a lot of manual coordination across different platforms. We want them to be able to keep a consistent presence, respond faster to audience activity, and reduce the effort involved in planning and publishing campaigns.
The most important capabilities are connecting external social accounts, creating and scheduling campaigns for multiple networks at once, managing contributor, approver, and publisher roles, and handling responses to comments or messages. It’s also important to monitor keywords and keep a clear history of campaigns so teams can track what was done and learn from it.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What are the rules and workflow for content approval before a campaign or post is published—for example, who can submit, who must review or approve, whether multiple approvals are needed, and what happens if content is edited after approval?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Typically, contributors can draft and submit content, but they shouldn’t be able to publish it directly unless they also have publisher rights. Approvers review the content before it goes live, and in most cases we’d expect a single approval step, though I could see some businesses wanting a second approval for sensitive campaigns. If content is edited after approval, it should go back into review because the approved version has changed.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What conditions or criteria should cause a campaign or post to require additional approval beyond the normal single review, such as a second approval, escalation to a higher reviewer, or special handling for sensitive content?
turns.interviewee_utterance: I’d expect extra approval for anything high-risk or brand-sensitive, like regulated promotions, pricing changes, legal statements, crisis-related posts, or content that mentions a major partner or public issue. We’d also want additional review if the post is going to a very large audience, has paid promotion attached, or uses material that isn’t fully standardized, like user-generated content or a controversial topic. The exact thresholds aren’t fully defined yet, so those rules would probably need to be configurable by the business.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What parts of the approval policy should be configurable by the business—such as by customer, brand, campaign type, region, audience size, channel, or risk level—and how should those configurations interact when more than one rule applies?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, those should all be configurable because different customers and brands will have different risk tolerances. I’d expect the rules to vary by customer, brand, campaign type, region, channel, and maybe audience size or risk level, with the business able to set stricter rules for sensitive combinations. When multiple rules apply, the safest rule should win, so if one rule says one approval and another says two, it should require two.

turns.interviewer_utterance: When multiple approval policy rules apply at the same time, how should Mashbot determine which rule takes precedence—for example, should the strictest rule always override, or do you want any explicit priority order, tie-breakers, or exceptions for certain rule types?
turns.interviewee_utterance: The strictest rule should generally override because that’s the safest and easiest for staff to understand. If two rules conflict at the same level, I’d want a clear priority order defined by the business, but I don’t think we need a lot of exceptions unless there’s a legal or compliance rule that must always win. In those cases, compliance should take precedence over everything else.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Which sources should Mashbot use to determine compliance and legal requirements for approval and publishing decisions—for example, internal policy documents, jurisdiction-specific regulations, industry standards, customer-provided rules, or external legal feeds?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Mashbot should be able to use internal policy documents and customer-provided rules first, because those are the most practical sources for day-to-day approval decisions. For legal and compliance, it should also respect jurisdiction-specific regulations and any industry standards that the customer has said apply to them. I’m not sure we’d need external legal feeds at launch, since that sounds more like an advanced feature unless we have a way to keep it reliable and maintained.

turns.interviewer_utterance: When Mashbot connects to external social networks, what API access constraints and failure-handling behavior should it support—for example, which platforms or permission limits must be respected, and what should happen if an account connection attempt fails, times out, or an access token expires?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Mashbot has to respect whatever permissions each network allows, so it may not always get the full set of publishing or reading rights on every platform. At a minimum, it should handle the common networks customers use, but the exact platform list and limits will depend on what those APIs support at the time. If a connection fails or times out, the user should get a clear error and be able to retry, and if a token expires, Mashbot should prompt for reconnection and avoid trying to publish until access is restored.

turns.interviewer_utterance: How should Mashbot handle approval and compliance policy history over time—for example, should it keep versioned policies with an audit trail of who changed what and when, how should overlapping policy scopes be evaluated, and what exceptions should occur if a compliance rule cannot be applied or conflicts with another rule?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, it should keep versioned policies with a full audit trail of who changed them and when, because that’s important for accountability and troubleshooting. For overlapping scopes, I’d expect the most specific policy to apply first, and then the stricter rule if there’s still a conflict. If a compliance rule can’t be applied or conflicts with another rule, Mashbot should block publishing by default and flag it for manual review rather than guessing.
